history: Cão is Latin canem, ‘dog’. Like pão from panem, it lost its final n but kept the nasal sound in the vowel, and the plural is cães. Spanish had the same old word, can, but replaced it in everyday speech with perro, a word of unknown origin. Portuguese stayed loyal to the Latin dog. Here Portugal and Brazil differ. In Portugal o cão is the normal word, and a cachorro is a puppy. In Brazil cachorro is the everyday word for any dog, and cão sounds rather formal. Latin canis also gave learned words: canino, ‘canine’, and the Canary Islands, Ilhas Canárias, named after dogs, not after birds.
historyEinfach: Cão means ‘dog’. The word comes from Latin canem. The plural is cães. In Portugal, a cachorro is a young dog, a puppy. In Brazil, cachorro is the normal word for every dog. Spanish says perro, a different word.

elsewhere.text: Spanish replaced the Latin dog with a word nobody has been able to explain.
French chien is the same Latin dog, with a softer start.
